title: Shemini Atzeret: stay one more day
hook: Rashi: like a king who asks his children to stay one more day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hoshana Rabbah, seven circuits and a bundle of willows. Your line was beat the willows. Today, the day after the festival ends, that isn't quite over.

The bags are by the door. The car is packed. Somebody has already said, we should really get going. And then a grandmother, or an aunt, or a parent who doesn't say this kind of thing out loud, says: stay. Just one more night. Nothing planned, no outing, no big meal. They just aren't ready for the house to be empty yet. The Torah's festival calendar has a day like that, right at the end of Sukkot. It has few rituals of its own, and a well-known explanation of it is a story about a family that doesn't want to say goodbye.
screen: `THE BAGS ARE BY THE DOOR.` → `STAY. JUST ONE MORE NIGHT.` → `A DAY WITH FEW RITUALS.`

segments.voice: Shemini Atzeret means the eighth day of assembly. In the old Jewish translation of Leviticus, after seven days of Sukkot, "on the eighth day shall be a holy convocation unto you," and then: "it is a day of solemn assembly." That's the word atzeret. Rashi hears in it holding back: I have held you here with me. Here's the strange part. The eighth day has no sukkah requirement, no lulav, no willows. In the Land of Israel, people step out of the booth and back into the house. So what is the day for? Rashi answers with a parable drawn from the midrash. A king invites his children to a feast for a set number of days. When it's time for them to leave, he says: your parting is hard for me. Please, stay one more day. That's the whole holiday. A week of crowds, guests, palm branches and booths, then one quiet day that's only about being together. The Talmud adds another layer. Over the seven days of Sukkot, the Temple offered seventy bulls, and the rabbis connected those seventy to the seventy nations of the world. On the eighth day, a single bull: a small, private meal after the big banquet. Today the day has one notable addition. In the standing prayer, people begin to mention rain, and many synagogues chant a special prayer for it. Winter is coming in the Land of Israel. The asking begins on the day when nobody is in a hurry to leave.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY OF ASSEMBLY.` · `NO BOOTH, NO LULAV, NO WILLOWS.` · `A KING SAYS: STAY ONE MORE DAY.` · `SEVENTY BULLS, THEN ONE.` · then, large: `STAY ONE MORE DAY.`

segments.voice: Bring one person you love to mind, near or far, and picture the last time you said goodbye, how quickly it went. Now imagine you stayed: no plan, no agenda, just the two of you in the same room. Breathe with that.
Shemini Atzeret. The eighth day of assembly, the day God, in Rashi's parable, asks the children to stay. Today's word.
Your line: stay one more day. Some days are only for being together. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Shemini Atzeret is a full festival day after Sukkot, kept with festive meals and synagogue services; the prayer for rain (Tefillat Geshem) is chanted, and the mention of rain enters the daily Amidah from that day until Passover.
